scope: Four explicitly reconstructed educational models; not empirical validation

changes.before: The original 1927 SIR epidemic model by Kermack and McKendrick, foundational for mathematical epidemiology. Introduced the concept of epidemic threshold (R0) and herd immunity. The basis for all modern compartmental disease models. Reference: Kermack, W. O., & McKendrick, A. G. (1927). A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics. Proceedings of the Royal Society A, 115(772), 700-721. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1927.0118
changes.after:
Educational constant-rate SIR example corresponding to the special case in Kermack and McKendrick (1927), equation 29. The parameters are illustrative; this does not reproduce their observed epidemic data. Reproduction-number diagnostics are derived for this homogeneous closed population.

Review 2026-10-20: repaired two diagnostic references to the existing reproduction-number variable. The dynamics implement the constant-rate SIR special case (Kermack-McKendrick 1927, equation 29), with illustrative parameters. This is not a reproduction of their observed epidemic data or a calibrated forecast. The default integrator is explicitly RK4 at the existing time grid, checked against an independent high-accuracy solution over the complete trajectory. Numerical accuracy does not establish empirical validity.

changes.before: Roy Anderson and Robert May's foundational work on herd immunity thresholds and vaccination programs. Shows how the critical vaccination coverage needed for disease elimination depends on R0, forming the basis for vaccination policy. Reference: Anderson, R. M., & May, R. M. (1991). Infectious Diseases of Humans. Oxford University Press.
changes.after:
Illustrative homogeneous SIR vaccination model with births, using herd-immunity concepts discussed by Anderson and May (1985). This is not their age-structured model, fitted data or a vaccination-policy forecast. Births without mortality, vaccination efficacy and the fixed rates are explicit educational assumptions.

Review 2026-10-20: repaired two diagnostic references to the existing Basic R0 variable. This homogeneous illustrative vaccination model is not the age-structured model or fitted data in Anderson-May (1985). Births without mortality and the illustrative efficacy/rates remain explicit assumptions; numerical and population-balance checks do not establish calibration. The default integrator is explicitly RK4 at the existing time grid, checked against an independent high-accuracy solution over the complete trajectory. Numerical accuracy does not establish empirical validity.

changes.before: Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered compartmental model with latent period. Extends SIR by adding an Exposed compartment for the incubation period when individuals are infected but not yet infectious. Reference: WHO Disease Outbreak Information. Source: https://www.who.int/
changes.after:
Illustrative closed Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered compartmental model with a latent period. Hethcote (2000) provides conceptual background. Initial exposed individuals come from the existing Initial Exposed parameter and the remainder start susceptible. The coefficients are not WHO data or a verified parameter set from the cited review.

Review 2026-10-20: reconstructed the closed SEIR initial state using the already supplied Total Population and Initial Exposed parameters; infectious and recovered remain zero. Corrected the diagnostic R0 reference and the DOI to match the named Hethcote review. The values are illustrative, not WHO data, calibration or a reproduction of a paper-specific parameter set. The default integrator is explicitly RK4 at the existing time grid, checked against an independent high-accuracy solution over the complete trajectory. Numerical accuracy does not establish empirical validity.

changes.before: Foundational neoclassical model of long-term economic growth. Capital accumulation drives growth in output per worker, but diminishing returns to capital mean the economy converges to a steady state. Long-run growth requires technological progress. Reference: Solow, R. M. (1956). A contribution to the theory of economic growth. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 70(1), 65-94. DOI: https://doi.org/10.2307/1884513
